cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example, at the depth the page prints
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes '=FISHERINV(0.972955)' with the result 0.75. Re-derived independently with mpmath at 50 decimal digits from the documented inverse transformation, the hyperbolic tangent: tanh(0.972955) = 0.74999996739414839198. That is NOT 0.75 -- the published "0.75" is a 2-decimal presentation, because the page's argument 0.972955 is itself a 6-decimal rounding of FISHER(0.75) = 0.97295507452765665255. This case asserts the published figure at the 2 decimals it is actually printed to; the companion case below asserts the true value at full depth.

cases.description: The same example at eight decimals, where the rounded argument shows
cases.expected_note: tanh(0.972955) = 0.74999996739414839198 (mpmath, 50 dps), i.e. 0.74999997 at 8 dp. Asserted separately from the documented 2-decimal figure so the assertion depth is auditable rather than arbitrary: an engine that returned a literal 0.75 here would be wrong, not precise.

cases.description: The documented inverse identity, exercised without the rounded intermediate
cases.expected_note: Microsoft documents the pair as "If y = FISHER(x), then FISHERINV(y) = x". Composing them directly avoids the 6-decimal truncation the published example carries, so the identity can be asserted at 12 decimals: tanh(atanh(0.75)) = 0.75. This is the case that actually tests the documented relationship rather than the page's rounding.

Derived from the documented inverse transformation: tanh(0) = 0 exactly. Asserted without a ROUND() wrapper because the value is exact, which catches an engine whose series expansion is not odd-symmetric at the origin.
Excel documents: "If y is nonnumeric, FISHERINV returns the #VALUE! error value."
